lead: A concrete mix or a steel bar does not have one fixed strength. Test results scatter. Limit state design starts from a cautious value near the weak end of that scatter: the characteristic strength. Loads also scatter, so design uses a characteristic load near the high end. These two numbers are the raw inputs; partial safety factors later turn them into design values (Chapter 1.6). The idea exists because safety must be based on measured variability, not on a single average.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.4 for the limit state idea and Chapter 1.1 for the material behaviour.

sections.h3: Scatter is real: the lower tail for strength

blocks.text: Characteristic strength is the strength value below which not more than 5% of test results fall. For concrete, fck is the 28-day cube strength measured on 150 mm cubes. The grade M25 means fck = 25 N/mm². For steel, fy is the characteristic yield strength; Fe 415 means fy = 415 N/mm².

Test results from one mix form a distribution. The mean μ is the average. The standard deviation σ measures the spread: a large σ means the mix is less consistent. If the distribution is close to normal, the 5% lower fractile lies about 1.65 standard deviations below the mean.

blocks.where: μ is the mean cube strength in N/mm²; σ is the standard deviation in N/mm²; f<sub>ck</sub> is the characteristic cube strength in N/mm². The multiplier 1.65 is the normal-distribution 5% fractile, rounded.

blocks.text: Why 1.65? For a normal curve, the area below μ − 1.65σ is about 5%. Design only needs the weak tail, because a few low cubes should not make the whole structure unsafe. The mean would put about half the tests below the design starting point, which is not cautious enough.

Some syllabi call these characteristic values. The same statistical idea is used for steel, where tensile tests give a lower 5% fractile. The stress–strain curves in Chapter 1.1 use these strengths as their labels.

sections.h3: Characteristic loads use the upper tail

blocks.text: Loads also scatter. The weight of a slab, the crowd on a balcony, the wind on a hoarding, and the water in a tank all vary. Characteristic load Qk is a load value with a small probability, usually 5%, of being exceeded in service. For a normal load model the 5% upper fractile is Qk = μQ + 1.65σQ, where μQ is the mean load and σQ is its standard deviation in the same units.
Notice the sign. Concrete and steel use the lower tail: μ − 1.65σ. Loads use the upper tail: μ + 1.65σ. A load that is too high is the unsafe case; a material that is too weak is the unsafe case.

Dead load is often calculated from dimensions and density, so its scatter is small. Live load has larger scatter. Wind and earthquake loads are treated with separate statistical models and return periods. The common thread is the same: pick a fractile, not the average.
Chapter 1.6 applies partial safety factors to these characteristic values.

Read f<sub>ck</sub> = 25 N/mm² as: 'if we test many cubes from this concrete, about 5 in 100 may be weaker than 25 N/mm².' Read Q<sub>k</sub> = 120 kN as: 'in service, the load is expected to exceed 120 kN only about 5% of the time.'

The characteristic value is not the design value. Design values are fck/γm and γfQk; the factors γm and γf are in Chapter 1.6. This separation is deliberate: one number describes the material or load; another number describes the required safety.

Standard grades are convenient labels for f<sub>ck</sub>. If a calculation gives 25.4 N/mm², M25 is chosen, not M30. Rounding down keeps the specified grade on the safe side of the calculated fractile.

figure.caption: Cube strengths from one mix form a bell curve. The marked point is the 5% lower fractile, f<sub>ck</sub> = 25.4 N/mm², not the mean of 32 N/mm².

spec.aria: A bell-shaped distribution of cube strengths centred at 32 N/mm² with a marked lower-tail point at 25.4 N/mm².

examples.question: Twenty-eight-day cube tests on concrete give a mean strength of 32 N/mm² and a standard deviation of 4 N/mm². Estimate the characteristic cube strength using the 5% fractile rule. State the nearest standard grade.
steps: Identify the mean μ = 32 N/mm² and the standard deviation σ = 4 N/mm².
For a normal distribution the 5% lower fractile is μ − 1.645σ; use 1.65 as the textbook rounding.
Round down to the standard grade M25, which has f<sub>ck</sub> = 25 N/mm².
examples.answer: f<sub>ck</sub> = 25.4 N/mm²; round down to grade M25.
examples.check:
mean = 32.0
sigma = 4.0
fck = mean - 1.65 * sigma
print(round(fck, 1))

code.code:
mean = 32.0
sigma = 4.0
fck = mean - 1.65 * sigma
print(round(fck, 1))

traps: Do not take the average cube strength as f<sub>ck</sub>. f<sub>ck</sub> is the 5% lower fractile, below the mean.
Do not use μ − 1.65σ for loads. Loads use the upper tail, μ + 1.65σ, because a high load is unsafe.
Keep units with μ and σ. Adding a strength in N/mm² to a load in kN is meaningless.
Characteristic values are not design values. The factors γ<sub>m</sub> and γ<sub>f</sub> are applied later, in Chapter 1.6.
When rounding to a standard grade, round down. A calculated 25.4 N/mm² does not justify calling the concrete M30.

quiz.q: Define characteristic cube strength of concrete.
quiz.a: The 28-day cube strength below which not more than 5% of test results fall.

quiz.q: Why is the mean cube strength not used as f<sub>ck</sub>?
quiz.a: The mean is the centre of the scatter; about half the tests fall below it. Design needs a cautious lower fractile, so f<sub>ck</sub> is set at the 5% lower tail.

quiz.q: Cube tests give mean 40 N/mm² and standard deviation 5 N/mm². Estimate f<sub>ck</sub> using the 5% fractile rule.
quiz.a: f<sub>ck</sub> = 40 − 1.65 × 5 = 40 − 8.25 = 31.75 N/mm². Nearest lower standard grade is M30.

quiz.q: A live load model has mean 100 kN and standard deviation 15 kN. Estimate the 5% upper-fractile characteristic load.
Mix A has mean 35 N/mm² and σ = 3 N/mm². Mix B has mean 35 N/mm² and σ = 6 N/mm². Which mix gives the higher f<sub>ck</sub>, and why?
quiz.a: A gives 35 − 4.95 = 30.05 N/mm²; B gives 35 − 9.9 = 25.1 N/mm². Lower scatter raises the 5% fractile for the same mean.

quiz.q: A student says 'characteristic load = mean load − 1.65σ'. Correct the statement for an upper-tail load.
quiz.a: For a load, the unsafe case is a high load, so the characteristic load is the upper 5% fractile: Q<sub>k</sub> = μ<sub>Q</sub> + 1.65σ<sub>Q</sub>. The minus sign belongs to strength, not load.
Concrete with characteristic cube strength f<sub>ck</sub> = 25 N/mm² at 28 days.

quiz.q: Why are characteristic values not the final numbers used in design?
quiz.a: They describe the material or load only. Design must add partial safety factors for adverse variability, so design values are obtained from characteristic values using γ<sub>m</sub> and γ<sub>f</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. Full structural reliability replaces the single 1.65 multiplier with a reliability index β and a full probability model. Students who continue in this area meet Monte Carlo simulation, first-order reliability methods, and load models for wind and earthquake. Codes revise characteristic values as data improve, so the number in a design office is tied to the edition of the code in use. Search for 'structural reliability index', 'Monte Carlo simulation in concrete', and 'probabilistic load modelling'.
